en: The Dharma of the Śrīmālā-sūtra contains immeasurable and boundless merit. By [practicing it], one attains [the state of] non-attainment;

its beneficial merit is identical to the signless (*animitta*). From this point onward, it is clear that there is great benefit. Now, by raising up wisdom and eloquence regarding the signless, one gathers and encompasses the boundless.

The Buddha said to Śrīmālā: "Now you shall further explain the principle of the 'gathering and upholding of the true Dharma' as taught by all Buddhas... [omitted] ...which is designated as the One Vehicle, in order to clarify the understanding of emptiness."

Because this is the manifestation of the [true] characteristics, the Buddha commanded her to speak further. Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. You have encompassed that which is profound and vast; its seeking is perhaps boundless. May you deign to expound these benefits—will you not speak of them? She then addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, that which encompasses the True Dharma is the Mahāyāna; it encompasses the realization of emptiness."

This is precisely the emergence of characteristics from the Mahāyāna. Why? Because the realization of emptiness of the three vehicles emerges from this One Great Mahāyāna. The Mahāyāna gives birth to all wholesome dharmas—both mundane and supramundane—of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the three vehicles; the realization of emptiness of the three vehicles all issues forth from this principle.
The principle is that there is no emergence; awakening is identical to entry, and since entry is non-entry, there is nothing that is not entered.

Thus, the meaning of "one" and "three" cannot be otherwise. World-Honored One, just as the great lake Anavatapta gives rise to the eight great rivers, so too does this Mahāyāna give birth to all the wholesome dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, both mundane and supramundane; it is a source of springs, vast and deep, filled and flowing according to its capacity.
The flow differs according to its source,
yet it is not different from water; likewise,
the empty mind is profound and vast, acquiring names according to the practice it follows.
Names differ according to cultivation,
while empty understanding remains ever the same.
This sameness gives rise to difference, yet there is nothing that does not arise from this sameness, World-Honored One.

Furthermore, just as all seeds depend upon the earth to grow, so too do all the wholesome dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—whether mundane or supramundane—depend upon the Mahāyāna to increase; their arising is no different, and their growth is likewise the same.

Therefore, World-Honored One, to abide in the Mahāyāna and embrace the Mahāyāna is to abide in the two vehicles and embrace the two vehicles; all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas, when subsumed under their principles and designated by their names, are without difference.
As the World-Honored One has spoken of the six bases.
What are these six? They are:

the abiding of the True Dharma, the extinction of the True Dharma, the Prātimokṣa Vinaya, going forth, receiving full ordination, and for the sake of the Mahāyāna—these are the six bases taught. This is because the singular, ultimate path is not something that can be sought by those with inferior resolve.
By means of the provisional names of the three [vehicles], the ultimate unity is secretly expressed.
Therefore, it was previously stated that the three vehicles emerge from the single extreme;
now it is clarified that when the great is pointed out as being small, the intention is to lead toward the great.
The Great Vehicle is not small; it is what is called "Great. Why is this? Because the great and the small are different. Why is it said that the small is the Great?

Because the abiding of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is the Mahāyāna, therefore it is said that the abiding of the Mahāyāna is the abiding of the True Dharma. Because the extinction of the True Dharma is the Mahāyāna, therefore it is said that the extinction of the Mahāyāna is the extinction of the True Dharma. The principle of emptiness is profound and still, remaining unchanged through antiquity and the present.
When manifested, it is called "abiding";
when concealed, it is called "extinction.

How could there be these two dharmas—*prātimokṣa* and *vinaya*—of abiding and extinction that exist apart from the Mahāyāna? They are one in meaning though different in name; the prevention of transgressions constitutes *prātimokṣa*.
The discipline for treating transgressions is the Vinaya;
both of these are meanings of the Mahāyāna,
yet they are called by the name of the Hīnayāna, and thus it is said that their names differ.
The names differ, but the principle is one.

Therefore, that which is the Mahāyāna Vinaya is precisely the Mahāyāna study of prohibitions, remedies, and the transcendence of characteristics; it is the Mahāyāna study itself. Why is this? Because prohibitions and remedies originally arise from the Hīnayāna.

Why is this so? Because one leaves the household life based on the Buddha and receives full ordination (*upasampadā*), and because one preaches the Great [Vehicle] while relying upon it, there is no separate "Small" [Vehicle].
One abandons heterodoxy for the sake of leaving the household life.

Attaining the principle constitutes full completion; therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna code of conduct (*vṛtta-śīla*) is the *vinaya*, it is the renunciation, and it is the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*). Because the "small" has no distinction from the "small," the "great" is taken as the small. For this reason, an Arhat has no separate renunciation or full ordination. Why? Because an Arhat relies upon the Tathāgata for renunciation and full ordination. Since there is no distinction in the cause, their arising is identical in its destination.
Therefore, the meaning of the six sense bases is none other than the Mahāyāna.
Arhats take refuge in the Buddha; although Arhats have fear, the principles elucidated by the opening and closing of the aforementioned vehicle are entirely without distinction.
The following clarifies that the single manifestation of awakening has both exhaustion and non-exhaustion.
That which is exhausted is called a vehicle (*yāna*) with no remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*);
that which is not exhausted is called a vehicle with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*).
There are four other kinds:
first, fear;
second, birth-and-death.
There are three afflictions and four objects of knowledge;
this first section clarifies that there remains something further to be feared.
Now, those who cultivate the One Vehicle to transcend all marks do so seeking the bliss of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); yet, as they have not yet reached its ultimate fulfillment,
they harbor a sense of fear and seek only its cessation.

This mind relies upwardly upon the Great Awakened One. Why is this? A sutra states: "What fear can there be for an Arhat who has already attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? Yet, regarding all non-activities (*apravṛtti*), the Arhat dwells in a state of fearful apprehension, like a person holding a sword who intends to come and harm him. For those of the Two Vehicles, existence (*bhava*) is not yet exhausted and the unconditioned is not yet fully realized; thus, they harbor deep dread toward non-activity. Therefore, while the Arhat lacks ultimate bliss, because both existence and non-existence have been forever exhausted, his form and mind are tranquil and serene.
The signless and unconditioned are called the ultimate.
Why is it that an Arhat has not yet attained fearlessness, yet receives the name "ultimate"? Why is there no ultimate bliss?

World-Honored One, relying on that which is not sought as a refuge—just as sentient beings, being without refuge, experience various terrors, and because of those terrors seek a place of refuge—so too the Arhat possesses fear; because of this fear, he relies upon the Tathāgata. Having no other refuge to seek, he relies solely upon the Buddha alone.
Sentient beings have not yet awakened;

they fear this state and gradually lose [their resolve for] the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), as they have not yet been led to the ultimate. Because the World-Honored One has stated that Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas possess fear, he spoke extensively of the Śrāvakas in order to explain the meaning of taking refuge in the Great [Vehicle].
The following clarifies the practice of not exhausting fear.

For this reason, it also encompasses the two vehicles; thus, because Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have remaining births and their dharmas are not yet exhausted, they possess birth. Although the ultimate state of the two vehicles has four aspects which are termed "nirvāṇa," it is called "nirvāṇa without conditioned activity" (asaṃskṛta-nirvāṇa).

Among these, there are further dharmas; because the dharmas of existence have not yet been fully exhausted, there is the "arising of arising. Because the remaining Brahma-conduct has been accomplished, although it is pure, liberation is not yet complete; for while existence is exhausted, that which pertains to non-existence is not yet exhausted.

If existence and non-existence are both exhausted, it is called "purity. Because phenomena have not yet reached ultimate emptiness, there must be that which is to be practiced; because awakening has not yet fathomed the fundamental source, there must be a method of liberation. One must practice because one has not yet crossed over to the other shore; one must sever [delusions] because the continuity of future existence must be further severed.
Beyond this, there remain four further knowledges.
The first two clarify that what has been exhausted is not yet fully exhausted;
the latter two clarify that non-arising gives rise once more.

Because it arises without being exhausted, there is future existence (*punarbhava*) that is not exhausted; because it is not severed, one remains far from the realm of nirvāṇa. When future existence continues, birth and death are endless;
thus, one is distant from nirvāṇa. Why is this? The first five phrases are originally names for "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

Why is it said now that there is a "remainder"? It is because only the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, attains parinirvāṇa by accomplishing all merits; whereas Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas do not accomplish all merits. To say they attain nirvāṇa is the Buddha’s skillful means to manifest the ultimate. To clarify the state of having a remainder: when the mind is extinguished in accordance with the profound principle, this is called the mark of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbuddha). When extinction itself is extinguished, this is called attaining nirvāṇa.

The exhaustion of all existence is called "nirvāṇa"; the non-arising [of existence] means "my births have already ended. Although the followers of the Two Vehicles have not yet exhausted all existence, they receive the name "nirvāṇa" because the final state is used to lead toward the initial state, drawing them far toward the state of non-arising.

This indicates that birth is not yet exhausted, meaning there remains further existence above. Only the Tathāgata attains parinirvāṇa and accomplishes immeasurable merit; whereas Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas accomplish only measurable merit. To say they "attain nirvāṇa" is a skillful means of the Buddha. Having reached the limit of unconditioned, immeasurable practice, and being able to exhaust ignorance, their holy life is established.

This explains that the aforementioned holy life (*brahmacarya*) was not pure; for only the Tathāgata attains *parinirvāṇa* and accomplishes inconceivable merit. Thus, when it is said that Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas accomplish conceivable merit and attain *nirvāṇa*, this is the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya*). "Inconceivable" refers to the perfect integration of existence and non-existence.
If one’s practice can penetrate through [to the goal], then what was to be done has already been accomplished.

This explains the preceding point: that there is something yet to be done; only a Tathāgata attains parinirvāṇa, having completely extinguished all faults that ought to be abandoned and having achieved the foremost purity. As for Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, they possess residual faults and are not of the foremost purity; those who claim to have attained nirvāṇa do so as a skillful means of the Buddha, in order to bring all continuities to an end and their cessation.

Regarding the subsequent absence of further existence (*anupādi-śeṣa*): it was explained above that there must be something to be abandoned; only the Tathāgata attains parinirvāṇa, being gazed upon by all sentient beings and transcending the realms of Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas. Therefore, while Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas remain distant from the realm of nirvāṇa despite cultivating the first four virtues, they have not yet been able to provide this explanation, as they are surpassed by those of the three vehicles and two vehicles.
Since it has been clarified above that the distance from the realm of nirvana at the beginning and end is manifest, it follows that there is still more to be explained.

As for the statement that Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, having observed liberation through the four knowledges, ultimately attain a place of rest—this too is the Tathāgata’s skillful means, an incomplete teaching of provisional meaning. Regarding these three phrases, the word "ultimately" is mentioned first.
Now, I shall clarify the meaning of these three remaining [categories] which open the way for the subsequent three chapters.
Thus, by enumerating them, one observes that liberation opens the way for the existence of afflictions (*kleśa-bhava*),
while the four ultimate knowledges (*jñāna*) open the way for the existence of the knowable (*jñeya-bhava*), thereby attaining a place of rest.
Regarding the statement that there is "a remainder" in death: for what reason? Because the principle has not yet been fully exhausted, how could it be said that death is ultimate?

There are two kinds of death; what are the two? They are called *pariccheda-maraṇa* (death by segmentation) and *acintya-nirmāṇa-maraṇa* (inconceivable transformative death). The following explains that liberation from *pariccheda-maraṇa* serves as a place of respite.
The severance of the four stages of abiding (catur-vāsa-bhūmi) is the contemplation for liberation;
there are those who take the Four Truths (catuḥ-satya) as the four wisdoms.
These three meanings are fully encompassed within the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
Therefore, through skillful means, all are designated as "ultimate.
This initial [explanation]—that birth has already ended while there remains a residual self—is a meaning that applies to all four gates.

For this reason, what is clarified here is only the existence of death with remainder. Those who undergo death in fragments are called deluded sentient beings; those who undergo inconceivable transformation and death are called Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of great power. As for "fragmented," it refers to the characteristics of the distinction between existence and non-existence.
Now, one obtains a fruit from a cause,
and the fruit receives its name according to that cause.
Therefore, by falsely grasping at the causes of existence and non-existence, one attains their distinctions.
The retribution of existence and non-existence is termed "segmented birth and death" (*paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa*).
Through the realization of emptiness and signlessness, one attains the inconceivable retribution;
yet, because this retribution has not yet exhausted the fundamental principle (*mūla*), it remains so.
There is a principle of transformation.
What is called "inconceivable transformative death" (acintya-pariṇāmi-cyuti) is categorized as being like the mind;

therefore, it is termed the "mind-made body" (manomaya-kāya). This continues until the ultimate, unsurpassed Bodhi, where Bodhi is quiescent and one is forever free from this affliction; hence, it is called "ultimate."

From this point downward, following these [stages], the occurrence of transformations has not been absent. Among the two kinds of death, because of the death of segmented existence (*pariccheda-maraṇa*), it is said that for Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, "my births are exhausted. This is because the wisdom of the Two Vehicles has already exhausted the grasping at the false.

Because one who is without further分段生 (segmented birth) can also realize the remaining fruit, it is said that "the holy life has been established. Among those who have exhausted [defilements], there is the realization of awakening; it is said that "the holy life has been established" because ordinary persons and gods cannot accomplish this. Since the seven types of trainees (*śaikṣa*) have abandoned the previously uncreated, deceptive afflictions, it is said that "what was to be done has been accomplished. This refers exclusively to the fruits of the two vehicles.
Wisdom can exhaust all that is false and deceptive; what remains below this level has not yet been discerned.

Because Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) and can no longer undergo further existence, it is said they "will not undergo further existence. Since the seeds [of existence] have already been exhausted and will not again produce fruit in the future, it is said they "will not undergo further existence. This does not mean that all afflictions are entirely exhausted, nor does it mean that all modes of rebirth are entirely ended; rather, it is stated that they "will not undergo further existence" because the exhaustion of the seeds is not yet universal.

Why is it that the causal continuity of what has already arisen does not cease, resulting in the formation of future existence (*punarbhava*)? It is because afflictions exist which cannot be severed by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas; these arise from deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) regarding the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Next, the remaining afflictions are explained.
There are certain subtle impurities and dual wheels that are understood only by the Greatly Awakened One and cannot be severed by those of the Two Vehicles.
Although the principle is profound and mysterious, I shall attempt to speak of it for now.
Life and death are vast and obscure, such that their beginning cannot be sought; they are eternally quiescent, empty, and subtle, such that their end cannot be discerned.
Although it is difficult to clarify the beginning and the end,
there is a way to approach them:
birth and death arise from the mind of appearances, while nirvana lies in wondrous awakening.
If one's realization has not yet exhausted the fundamental principle, there will inevitably be attachments to signs.
These are twofold: first, false existence;
second, false non-existence.
The delusive conditioned is coarse;
the delusive unconditioned is subtle.
If one awakens to the principle, the darkness is removed and the subtle is severed.

Because the followers of the Two Vehicles have not yet exhausted the state of non-existence (*anabhāva*), there remains that which is not severed, namely the ground of the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*). There are two kinds of afflictions (*kleśa*): what are the two? They are the afflictions of the dwelling ground (*vāsabhūmi-kleśa*) and the arising afflictions (*utthāna-kleśa*). Regarding these afflictions, there are two types of intensity—subtle and gross—and likewise two types regarding their arising or non-arising.
The reason for this is that grasping at false principles is "view," becoming defiled by attachment to phenomena is "craving," and failing to recognize the true nature of reality is "ignorance."
Because craving and views are deluded regarding the principle and are further accompanied by grasping, they are called "heavy.
Ignorance, however, simply fails to recognize the principle and has nothing else to which it is specifically attached; therefore, it is called "light and subtle."

Within each of the two categories—the light and the heavy—there are respective *sthāna-bhūmi* (abiding grounds) and *kleśa-samudācāra-sthāna-bhūmi* (grounds for the arising of afflictions). There are four such grounds; what are the four? They are: the ground of abiding in the view of a single locus (*ekadeśa-dṛṣṭi-sthāna-bhūmi*), the ground of craving for desire (*kāmarāga-sthāna-bhūmi*), the ground of craving for form (*rūparāga-sthāna-bhūmi*), and the ground of craving for existence (*bhavarāga-sthāna-bhūmi*). Indeed, the arising of the bonds and burdens [of saṃsāra]...
Because birth necessarily arises from conditions, there are four names.
First, because it arises in common with delusion regarding principle (*tattva*), it is called "one" (*eka*).
Second, because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises according to objects, it receives its name by following the respective realms (*dhātu*).
Therefore, attachment is collectively categorized as the four abodes (*catur-vihāra*).
These four are "abodes" (*vihāra*) because they each maintain their own respective divisions as objects of perception;

they are "grounds" (*bhūmi*) because they are capable of giving rise [to further states]. All that arises from these four abodes constitutes the arising of afflictions. This "arising" refers to the mind at every moment (*kṣaṇa*), its associated mental factors, and those which are triggered by pure conditions. It is designated as "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) because it is a temporary convergence.

That is to say, taking that mind as the object of association—whereas the World-Honored One’s mind is non-associated—the ground of abiding in ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-anuśaya*) is also either an object of perception but not termed "associated," or it has existed throughout vast eons; hence it is called "beginningless" (*anādi*).
Because it is the condition for delusion regarding the principle, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

Regarding those that are dissociated: the first four dwelling-grounds (*paryavasthāna*) are dissociated; when the four dwelling-grounds arise, they are associated, and when the dwelling-ground of ignorance arises, it is also associated.
There are two kinds of association (*samprayoga*):
first, the mental factors (*caitasika*) arise and cease in association with their objects;
second, ignorance (*avidyā*) is associated with the mind.
Now it is clarified that "illumination" (ming) may be associated with the mind.
The mutual conditioning of the three realms constitutes the mind-consciousness (citta-vijñāna);
the emptiness of the essence of the Three Vehicles constitutes the wisdom-mind (prajñā-citta).
Because it arises within the four abiding characteristics, it is associated with the mind and consciousness;
being subtle, obscure, and distantly pervasive, it is also dim. That mental wisdom is thus characterized by association with the mental wisdom, wherein the hindrance is heavy.

The four abodes have their names stripped away and their characteristics removed; the wisdom-mind associated with ignorance is designated as "non-cognition. Thus, this wisdom is not without correspondence.
Therefore, the exhaustion of the four abodes and the ground of the abode of ignorance is not a state of correspondence.
The two types of arising are not mutually incompatible;
the same applies to ignorance being beginningless and the four abidings.
However, it is only from the arising of the four abidings [that the afflictions manifest].
Arising is not a constant arising;
ignorance is deluded regarding principle,
never for a moment failing to arise.
Arising does not arise constantly;
therefore, there is a beginning.
Yet, from the very beginning, it has never failed to arise.
Therefore, it is beginningless;
for this reason, the Dwelling Place of Ignorance is called "beginningless ignorance.
This dependent origination pervades all four dwelling places.
Within all minds— whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—
the [defilements] abide by virtue of their conditions and arise as mental concomitants by virtue of their origination.
Whether subtle or obscurely penetrating, it exists everywhere; its characteristics are released and named, and in principle, it also governs the subtle.

Once the subtle is manifested, it truly accords with its name. The afflictions of the four abodes pervade throughout consciousness and mind, yet they do not penetrate the wisdom of the mind. Those that arise from the associated [factors] exist only within their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and not in other minds.
Whether subtle or profound, the pervasive nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) extends throughout this;
whether manifest or differentiated, the conditions for its arising vary accordingly.

By this one may know that the power of the four abodes of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) in the World-Honored One surpasses all other afflictions; compared to these, the seeds and bases of all other afflictions cannot be reached by calculation or analogy. Thus ends the preceding section on the different names of the afflictions.
The following clarifies that the power [of ignorance] is unequal: that which arises from the stages (*bhūmi*) is superior;
that which relies upon conditions as its support and arises in a manner similar [to them] is the seed.
Because this briefly cites dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is said to be "based on seeds" (*bījāśrita*), by which one may infer the power of ignorance.

When the characteristics of that which is beyond the reach of power are manifested, it can be calculated; however, the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) is difficult to know. To cite existence (*bhava*) as a comparison for non-existence—how could they possibly be equal?

World-Honored One, such is the power of the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*); compared to the four grounds of abiding categorized under craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), its power is the greatest. Thus, by comparing the seeds upon which the four grounds depend with ignorance, [the latter is seen to be superior].

Now, by the power of ignorance, it surpasses the four abodes; let me illustrate this with a metaphor. For example, just as the evil Māra Pāpīyas possesses sovereignty over the power, lifespan, retinue, and requisites of the gods of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven—such that his sovereignty is preeminent—so too is the power of the ground of ignorance (avidyāvāsabhūmi) most supreme among the four grounds of abiding in existence and craving (*bhavarāga*). Just as the celestial Māra occupies the honored position and leads those below, so does ignorance govern the root from which the branches proceed.
How could this be possible for those at the stage of the four abidings?

Therefore, it is superior. Even the afflictions based on the number of sands of the Ganges, as well as the four kinds of afflictions that have long resided and the associated afflictions arising from the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-anuśaya*), [are overcome by it].
It cannot be called by the name "Ganges Sands" merely because it is unified as one,
nor because it may have reached its end at some point in the past.

It causes the branches and twigs to persist for a long time; that which cannot be severed by the wisdom of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas can only be severed by the Bodhi-wisdom of the Tathāgata—such is the darkness of profound obscurity.
It is not illuminated by a flickering candle;

only the Great Awakened One can illuminate its profound darkness. Thus, World-Honored One, the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is the most powerful force, and it is only the Buddha who can sever it—this may indeed be called "great. World-Honored One, it is as if one were to take conditions and the causes of tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*) to produce the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātu*), thereby manifesting their power.
Now, its function will be clarified;

this also explains the preceding phrase, "not exhausting the taking of birth. Thus, with the ground of ignorance as the condition and uncontaminated karma as the cause, the three kinds of mind-made bodies of Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and powerful Bodhisattvas are produced. The four graspings serve as the conditions for the limited分段 (segmented) birth.
Ignorance serves as the moisture for transformation;
although it is absent within the *ālayavijñāna*,
it has not yet reached its ultimate exhaustion within the *manas*.
Because they have not yet reached the ultimate refinement of those three stages, it causes the rebirths of those in the three vehicles to be inexhaustible.

Therefore, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the condition for the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*) and untainted karma (*anāsravakarman*). In those three stages, the arising of the three kinds of mind-made bodies and the arising of untainted karma depend upon the ground of the abode of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*); they are not without conditions. Thus, the three—the three kinds of mind-made bodies, untainted karma, and the ground of the abode of ignorance—do not arise independently of one another.

Arising must necessarily follow from conditions; the Dwelling Place of Ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*) is the third of these conditions. World-Honored One, thus there are four dwelling places, including the Dwelling Place of Craving (*tṛṣṇā-āśraya*), whose functions do not coincide with those of the Dwelling Place of Ignorance; this clarifies the difference between their respective roles in initiating and moistening birth.

Now, let us clarify why the distinctions between cessation and extinction are not the same: the ground of the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) differs from the four grounds of dwelling (*catur-vāsabhūmi*). It is severed at the stage of Buddhahood and severed by the wisdom of Buddha-enlightenment (*buddha-bodhi-jñāna*); whereas the two vehicles sever the four [grounds of dwelling] but do not sever ignorance.

The Buddha has severed ignorance; there are no four [stages] to be severed, which is why he is distinct. Why is this? Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas sever the four types of abiding grounds (*catur-vihāra-bhūmi*), yet their outflows (*āsrava*) are not exhausted, they do not attain sovereign power, and they do not realize [the ultimate]. The three stages mentioned above are divided into the three realms (*tridhātu*); the four abiding grounds involve the false grasping at existence.
The outflows that arise with respect to existence are called the realm of outflows (*sāsrava-dhātu*). The outflows that arise with respect to non-existence—
which is falsely grasped through the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*)—
are called the realm of no-outflows (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
In the stage of Buddhahood, the quiescence of both existence and non-existence constitutes the realm of nirvana.

Therefore, although those of the two vehicles have severed the outflows of existence (āsrava), they have not yet severed the outflows of non-existence; thus it is said that their "outflows are not yet exhausted."
This is precisely the realm of ignorance (*avidyā-dhātu*). Because one is bound by subtle afflictions, one does not attain the realization of self-mastery.

If the realization of ignorance is not exhausted, what can be realized? That which is not exhausted of outflows (*anāsrava*) is precisely the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*). If that is not exhausted, then ignorance is not exhausted. World-Honored One, because Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas in their final birth are covered and obstructed by the ground of the abiding of ignorance, they do not know and do not awaken to those various dharmas. This is prior to the eighth stage and above among the Greatly Powerful Bodhisattvas.
This present final body is the very end of the Cloud of Dharma stage;
for it has been previously explained that ignorance moistens rebirth as clearly as if it were manifest.
Starting with great power,
one brings the investigation to the end of ignorance,
because it is understood that the subsequent existence is not yet exhausted.

At the stage of Buddhahood, one cannot perceive or cognize the mind; because of this lack of knowledge and vision, that which ought to be abandoned is not abandoned, and it is not brought to completion. Not seeing the Buddha-dharma, that which should be abandoned remains unabandoned.

Alternatively, because it is not yet severed, it is not ultimate; because it is not severed, it is called liberation with remainder (*sa-avaśeṣa*). It is not liberation free from all faults; thus, "my future existence" remains, which is called having remainder. It is called partial purification (*pariśuddhi*), not complete purification; thus, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has remainder. It is called the accomplishment of remaining merit, not the accomplishment of all merit; thus, that which was to be done has remainder. Because there is the accomplishment of remaining liberation, remaining purification, and remaining merit, one knows that suffering is partially severed, the origin is partially realized, cessation is partially attained, and the path is partially cultivated. Because afflictions are not exhausted, the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) remain; this is called attaining a small portion of nirvāṇa. One who attains a small portion of nirvāṇa is said to be "heading toward the realm of nirvāṇa. Because there is something penetrated, it is called a "small portion."
Because it ultimately leads to the final goal, it is said to "tend toward" [nirvana].
*Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*, Fascicle One. Offered by the disciple Tanshou Kedun.
